title: Factors Affecting Reaction Rates
lead: Five things set how fast a reaction goes: the nature of the reactants, how finely a solid reactant is divided, the temperature, the concentrations of the reactants and the presence of a catalyst.
objectives: Describe the effects of chemical nature, physical state, temperature, concentration, and catalysis on reaction rates
summary_html: The rate of a chemical reaction is affected by several parameters. Reactions involving two phases proceed more rapidly when there is greater surface area contact. If temperature or reactant concentration is increased, the rate of a given reaction generally increases as well. A catalyst can increase the rate of a reaction by providing an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy.

exercises.prompt: Describe the effect of each of the following on the rate of the reaction of magnesium metal with a solution of hydrochloric acid: the molarity of the hydrochloric acid, the temperature of the solution, and the size of the pieces of magnesium.

answer.solution: Higher molarity increases the rate of the reaction. Higher temperature increases the rate of the reaction. Smaller pieces of magnesium metal will react more rapidly than larger pieces because more reactive surface exists.

exercises.prompt: Explain why an egg cooks more slowly in boiling water in Denver than in New York City. (Hint: Consider the effect of temperature on reaction rate and the effect of pressure on boiling point.)

answer.solution: The egg cooks more slowly in Denver because water there boils at a lower temperature, and the reactions that cook the egg run more slowly at a lower temperature. A liquid boils when its vapor pressure equals the pressure of the atmosphere above it. Denver lies about a mile above sea level, where the atmospheric pressure is only about 83% of the pressure at sea level in New York City, so its water reaches that lower vapor pressure and boils at about 95 °C instead of 100 °C. Boiling water cannot get hotter than its boiling point, however strongly it is heated. Cooking an egg is a set of chemical reactions in which its proteins change structure, and chemical reactions typically occur faster at higher temperatures. In water about 5 °C cooler, those reactions are slower, so the egg takes longer to cook in Denver.

exercises.prompt: In the Sim of nitric oxide and ozone in a closed box, observe how the molecules collide and react under varying conditions. Set the temperature and the initial concentrations of each reactant, and watch the count of collisions above the graph and the concentration of ozone falling on it. How is the rate of the reaction affected by concentration and temperature?

answer.solution: The rate increases when the concentration of either reactant increases and when the temperature increases. At 300 K, a higher initial concentration of nitric oxide or of ozone puts more molecules in the box, so they meet more often: the collision count grows faster, more reactions occur in the same time, and the ozone concentration falls more steeply, giving a steeper dashed line and a larger average rate. Raising the temperature from 200 K to 600 K at 1.00 M of each reactant makes the molecules move faster, so they collide more often, and a larger share of those collisions react, so the ozone is again used up faster. Because a run holds only a few dozen collisions, single runs scatter, but repeated runs show both trends. Both agree with this section: rates usually increase when the concentration of a reactant increases, and reactions occur faster at higher temperatures.
